PM, Tue Sep 29 (as of 17:35 ET). The day's biggest move was in rates and oil, not equities. The US 2Y yield fell 5.4bp to 4.8765% while the 10Y was unchanged at 5.2362% and the 30Y rose 1.92bp to 5.5658%. That twist steepening points to markets pricing a Fed that is closer to done hiking, while term premium keeps building at the long end. Oil gave back ground: Brent fell 2.58% to $102.56 and WTI dropped 3.48% to $89.38, even though Washington is still rejecting Tehran's Hormuz proposal. Equities drifted lower on thin conviction: SPX -0.17% to 7670.84, Nasdaq -0.09%, Dow -0.26%, Russell -0.35%. Europe was split (SX5E +0.30%, FTSE -0.45%) and the Nikkei fell 0.60%. VIX was barely changed at 16.04. Credit softened at the margin (US HY OAS +9bp to 3.03%, EUR HY +6bp) but spreads remain near historic tights. Sentiment is complacent-but-cautious. Positioning looks like it is waiting on Micron (Wed after the close), this week's labor data and any Iran headline.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Today (US 1d) had a defensive tilt at the edges: Utilities +1.14%, Comm Services +0.40% and Industrials +0.19% led, while Energy -0.89% (tracking crude), Materials -0.55% and Staples -0.54% lagged. Over 1 month the rotation is clear. Only Info Tech (+4.1%) and Comm Services (+2.61%) are positive, while Materials (-6.95%), Financials (-6.83%), Cons Discr (-6.71%), Utilities (-6.57%) and Real Estate (-6.23%) sold off. Rate-sensitive and consumer cyclicals are being punished by a 5%+ 10Y, and mega-cap growth is the only shelter. Global sectors echo this: 1m Info Tech +3.68% and Comm Services +2.68%, Materials -7.78%, Cons Discr -6.68%. YTD leadership is Energy (US +34.64%, global +30.7%) and Info Tech (US +27.02%, global +34.13%), with Utilities (-8.06% US) and Cons Discr (-5.34% US) the laggards. Growth is beating value outside energy, and breadth is narrowing: a late-cycle pattern.

Key levels: US IG 100bp, reachable if Micron or the jobs data disappoint and equities correct 5-8% with the 10Y holding above 5%. US HY 350-400bp would require an oil re-spike from an Iran escalation or a growth scare that pushes defaults up. Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. This rule failed all three pre-registered gates as a tradable overlay (placebo p=0.465); do not size positions off it. See the monitor_spread skill (MONITOR_SPREAD.md).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.88 vol points (60th percentile of the 30 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 106.6 (77th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 107bp (steeper by 36bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.24%2026-09-29

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.24 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Sticky but cooling underneath. Headline-adjacent core PCE is still hot at 3.34% YoY and flexible prices are running 4.94% (energy pass-through from the Iran shock). But the robust central-tendency measures (median CPI 2.58%, trimmed-mean CPI 2.57%, trimmed-mean PCE 2.28%, core sticky CPI 2.70%) sit near the middle of their history and are mostly falling (per the computed Core-Trend Sub-Score). Breadth remains a concern: per the Dallas distribution, 52.2% of the PCE basket (computed: 9.3 + 13.0 + 29.9) is inflating faster than 3%, versus 25.8% falling. That argues the Fed cannot declare victory, but it does not support a runaway-inflation regime. Wages (AHE 3.1%) and breakevens (5y 2.351%) are not de-anchoring.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed dashboard says this cycle's excess sits in one place: semiconductors and AI infrastructure. Micron, now a roughly $1.2 trillion market cap on Bloomberg data and reporting Wednesday, is the poster child. Semis at 94% of 2000-peak P/E conditions is the only equity-froth gauge flashing red. Around it, the macro plumbing looks like late 1999: credit spreads tighter than 2000, financial conditions looser, VIX low, and commodities cheap versus stocks as capital crowds into equities. What is missing is euphoria and a trigger. Retail sentiment is net bearish, consumer confidence is subdued, the curve is not inverted and the PMIs are still rising. Unlike 2000, the Fed is hiking into 3%+ core PCE with a 5.24% 10Y, which pressures valuations from the discount-rate side rather than through a growth rollover. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, elevated long-term EPS-growth expectations) are approximate. They were not web-verified this session, since the search budget went to news, and should be treated as rough. They point to valuation-level risk comparable to or above 2000 on concentration and market cap/GDP, even as the broad P/E sits far below the 175x dot-com Nasdaq extreme. The 2000-02 template (-78% over 31 months, computed) is a tail, not a base case. The actionable read is concentration risk in semis around catalysts like MU.

⚔️Iran War

The US–Iran conflict remains in a no-war/no-peace standoff centered on the Strait of Hormuz. Last week Iran proposed a seven-day plan for a ceasefire and a phased reopening of Hormuz. The plan was contingent on the US meeting conditions from a mid-June memorandum of understanding that collapsed after several weeks, and Trump has publicly rejected it (CBS News; Al Jazeera live blog, Sep 26). Trump says negotiators are talking through mediators but insists he has 'offered them NOTHING' (CBS News). On Tuesday the IRGC said it is developing new weapons to defend the Islamic Republic, and Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran is prepared for war to resume 'even if it comes to a doomsday war' (CBS News / Al Jazeera). Al Jazeera coverage reported Brent rising more than 3% to top $107 after Washington dismissed Tehran's proposal. On Bloomberg's print today, Brent closed the session lower at 102.56 (-2.58%), so the market is fading the headline risk for now. That leaves room for a sharp re-rating if talks break down.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Oct 27–28 FOMC: hold at 3.75–4.00% is the base case (inferred). Warsh secured a unanimous 25bp hike in September. Analysts note a credible case for waiting in October to observe that hike's effects, and J.P. Morgan's next-hike forecast is December, not October. The inference rests on those sources plus today's 5.4bp rally in the 2Y.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from his Jackson Hole keynote and on-record positions: at most one or two more 25bp hikes (J.P. Morgan sees December but no extended cycle), then an extended hold while core PCE stays above 3%. Balance-sheet reduction from the $6.7T level is his structural priority, but it is stalled until the five task forces (communications, balance sheet, data, productivity, inflation framework) report early next year. Expect an active balance-sheet runoff/composition shift in 2027 that could lift term premium, consistent with today's 30Y rising while the 2Y fell.

Warsh has quickly established a hawkish, 'deliver price stability' identity. He held in July, gave a Jackson Hole speech that analysts said raised hike odds and could put the Fed 'at odds' with Treasury, and then delivered a unanimous hike in September, citing core PCE above 3% every month of 2026 and geopolitical developments. His signature agenda of a smaller Fed footprint, less forward guidance and a shrunken balance sheet is meeting internal resistance: July minutes showed colleagues wanting the task-force reviews completed first (CNBC Sep 25; Yahoo Finance). Flagged inference: the combination of rate hikes now and balance-sheet shrinkage later is bearish for the long end and supportive of curve steepening, even if the front end has peaked.
